title: data-storytelling Review: A Narrative Arc That Pushes Toward Drama
description: We used the data-storytelling skill to write a short post about our registry's numbers. Its structure gave the draft a clear order. Its push toward a dramatic climax produced one framing error, and it has no step for checking figures.

author.name: TrustedSkills Team
author.bio: We assess AI agent skills by installing them, running them against real work, and reading the source. We don't accept payment for reviews.

basisNote: Part of a batch of thirteen data and automation skills run on the same day against the same dataset: this site's own registry index, 26,001 skills in one 71 MB JSON file. Each run worked in its own private copy of the site's repository. One run on one dataset is one data point, not a benchmark.

runs.task: Write a 600 to 900 word data story for a possible "State of the registry" post: how many skills there are, how many install cleanly, how the verification tiers split, and which categories dominate. Follow the skill's narrative structure, take every number from a logged query, and do not claim causes the data cannot show.
runs.outcome:
`npx skills add wshobson/agents --skill data-storytelling` installed it first time.

The skill is structure and phrasing only: a story arc (hook, context, rising action, climax, resolution, call to action), a three-pillar table, and do's and don'ts. Its reference file adds worked examples, all built on invented business figures such as "We're losing $2.4M annually to preventable churn". It has no step for getting or checking the numbers, so the agent wrote its own query script and re-checked the headline figures in Python and with plain text search.

The 754-word draft follows the arc. The numbers are right: 26,001 skills, 18,513 (71.2%) with an install command that still resolves, 94.8% in the community tier, and three categories making up 51.2%. We re-counted these.

The climax is where it went wrong. To build a dramatic turn, the draft grouped `unverified` with `verified` and `featured` as "the tiers meant to signal the most trust". `Unverified` is the lowest tier. The draft also opens with "Here's the finding that matters most" and a "Worse:" beat. The skill's own advice on uncertainty (correlation is not causation) did keep the draft from inventing a cause.
runs.environment: Claude Code subagent (Sonnet 5) with the installed SKILL.md loaded as its instructions, in a private clone of the TrustedSkills website repo at commit 5169470. Queries in Node, cross-checked in Python.

summary: A short guide to shaping findings into a story: lead with the point, build to one main insight, end with an action. That gave our draft a clear order. The arc also wants a climax, and on data without one it pushed the draft to overstate a finding and mislabel a tier. There is nothing on checking numbers. Use it for structure, then do a plain-language pass for accuracy.

strengths.title: A clear structure to follow
strengths.body: Hook, context, rising action, climax, resolution, call to action. The draft never wandered.

strengths.title: Good caution on causes
strengths.body: Its advice on uncertainty kept the draft from inventing a reason for a pattern the data only showed.

strengths.title: Puts method after the point
strengths.body: "Don't show methodology first" moved the data note to one line under the title, which read better.

limitations.title: The arc rewards drama
limitations.body: It asks for a climax whether or not the data has one. Our draft grouped the lowest tier with the highest to build one.

limitations.title: No step for checking numbers
limitations.body: It assumes the figures are ready and right. Our run had to write and cross-check its own queries.

limitations.title: Examples use invented revenue figures
limitations.body: Every worked example is a SaaS story with made-up dollar amounts. There is no pattern for data with no money in it.

bestFor.title: Turning checked findings into a stakeholder update
bestFor.body: Have every figure checked before you start, and reread the climax for overstatement.

notFor: Anything where accuracy matters more than impact, such as a public report or a trust page, unless someone edits it for plain claims.
